hook.situation: You want to tell a Korean friend 'I drink coffee every morning.' You know the word 커피, you know 마셔요 — but you're not sure what goes between them. Is it 커피가? 커피는? 커피를? One small particle changes the entire grammatical logic of the sentence.
objectives: Attach 을 or 를 correctly after the object in any present-tense sentence
Say what you eat, drink, study, read, and write every day
Use the short negative (안) to say what you don't do
hook.whyItMatters: 을/를 is the particle that tells listeners WHAT is being acted on. Without it your sentences sound like a list of disconnected words. Once this clicks, you can build an unlimited number of complete action sentences — and Koreans will immediately know you understand Korean sentence structure.

grammarNotes.title: N을/를 — the object particle
grammarNotes.func: 을/를 marks the object of a sentence — the thing the action happens to (what you eat, drink, read, watch). It attaches to the noun that receives the verb's action, so it is the partner of every action verb you learn.

formTable.ex: 밥 → 밥을 · 책 → 책을 · 물 → 물을

formTable.when: Noun ends in a vowel (no 받침)
formTable.ex: 우유 → 우유를 · 커피 → 커피를 · 친구 → 친구를

examples.note: 밥 ends in a consonant (ㅂ 받침) → 을. 밥 is the object of 먹다.
물 ends in ㄹ 받침 (a consonant) → 을, not 를.
책 ends in ㄱ 받침 → 을. 보다 here means 'read / look at'.
친구 ends in a vowel (ㅜ), no 받침 → 를. 만나다 takes its object with 을/를, not 와/과.

keyPoint.label: Object 을/를 vs subject 이/가
keyPoint.body: 을/를 marks WHAT receives the action (the object); 이/가 marks WHO does it (the subject). In 친구가 밥을 먹어요 (A friend eats), 친구 is the doer → 가, and 밥 is the thing eaten → 을. Don't swap them. In casual speech Koreans often drop 을/를 (밥 먹어요), but learn to add it correctly first — the dropping comes naturally later.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 밥을 is pronounced [바블]: the final ㅂ links into the following vowel (linking, 연음). Likewise 책을 → [채글], 한국어를 → [한구거를].

drill.instruction: Add the right object particle and say the full sentence — follow the model.
drill.model: (물) 마셔요. → 물을 마셔요. · (커피) 마셔요. → 커피를 마셔요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: 저는 밥 먹어요 treated as the 'correct, complete' textbook form
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English has no object particle, so learners forget 을/를 and treat the bare noun as finished. The neutral, fully-formed sentence keeps the particle; dropping it is a casual-speech shortcut, not the default you should write.

grammarNotes.title: 안 + verb — the short negative
grammarNotes.func: 안 makes a verb negative — it means 'do not / does not'. You put 안 directly in front of the verb to say you don't do the action (안 먹어요 = I don't eat).

formTable.ex: 먹어요 → 안 먹어요 · 봐요 → 안 봐요 · 마셔요 → 안 마셔요

formTable.add: 안 goes between the noun and 하다
formTable.ex: 공부해요 → 공부 안 해요 · 운동해요 → 운동 안 해요

examples.note: 안 sits right before the verb 먹어요. The object 밥을 keeps its normal place.
안 negates the action 보다, not the object 책을.
With a 하다 verb, 안 splits in: 공부 안 해요, NOT 안 공부해요.

keyPoint.label: 안 (choose not to) vs 못 (can't) — preview
keyPoint.body: 안 means you simply don't / choose not to do something (안 먹어요 = I don't eat it). 못 means you're unable to even though you might want to (못 먹어요 = I can't eat it). Both go in front of the verb, but the meaning differs: 안 = won't / don't, 못 = can't. You'll practice 못 in its own chapter — for now just remember 안 is the everyday negative.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 안 + verb does not fuse: the ㄴ of 안 stays crisp and there is no tensing on the verb (안 봐요 = [안봐요], not [안뽜요]). Keep them as two clear beats.

drill.instruction: Make each sentence negative with 안 — follow the model. Watch the 하다 verb.
drill.model: 밥을 먹어요. → 밥을 안 먹어요. · 공부해요. → 공부 안 해요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English puts 'not' before the whole verb, so learners say 안 공부해요. But 공부하다 is noun(공부) + 하다, and 안 must slip between them: 공부 안 해요. This split only happens with 하다 verbs; ordinary verbs take 안 straight in front (안 먹어요).

grammarNotes.title: 자연스럽게 말하기 — How Korean actually sounds
grammarNotes.func: Korean squeezes its most common words the moment people speak, and those short forms are what fill KakaoTalk, subtitles, and everyday conversation. 저는 becomes 전, 것이 becomes 게, 무엇을 becomes 뭘. The meaning stays the same and so does the respect level — what shifts is how formal you sound, so these belong to speech rather than to a business email. You have just learned 은/는 and 을/를, so you can now see exactly what is being squeezed together.

formTable.ex: 전 학생이에요. ("I'm a student.") — 난 is the same squeeze on 나는, but this app sticks to 저/전.
넌 어디 가? ("Where are you going?") — 반말. Read it, don't say it: use 전 + 해요체 instead.
먹을 게 없어요. ("There's nothing to eat.") · 이걸 주세요. ("Give me this one.") · 이건 뭐예요? ("What's this?")
뭘 먹을까요? ("What shall we eat?") · 뭐가 맛있어요? ("What's tasty?") — 무엇 shrinks to 뭐 first, then 뭐+를 → 뭘; 뭐가 takes 가 because 뭐 ends in a vowel.
좋은 거 같아요. ("I think it's good.") — but write 좋은 것 같습니다 in an email or a report.

examples.note: 저는 → 전. The topic marker 는 collapses onto 저. Still 해요체, still polite — 전 is not more casual than 저는.
무엇을 → 뭘. In everyday conversation 뭘 (or 뭐) is the norm, even when you're being polite. 무엇을 isn't dead — it's just formal: you'll hear it from news anchors and in set service phrases like 무엇을 도와드릴까요?

examples.en: I think this is really tasty.
examples.note: 이것 → 이거, 것 같아요 → 거 같아요. Two contractions in one polite sentence — this is ordinary adult speech, not slang.

examples.en: It's a bit cold today, isn't it?
examples.note: -지요 → -죠. The full -지요 sounds stiff in conversation; -죠 is what you actually hear.

keyPoint.label: Shorter spelling, same politeness — but not the same formality
keyPoint.body: A contraction changes the spelling, not the meaning and not the level of respect: 전 학생이에요 and 저는 학생이에요 are equally polite, and 이거 주세요 is no ruder than 이것을 주세요. What it does change is how FORMAL you sound. Short forms are speech; the full forms are for writing and for formal rooms — a job interview, a presentation, a business email, an exam. Say 거 같아요 to a friend or a coworker, but write 것 같습니다 in that email. And one warning: none of this rescues 넌. 너 is a 반말 word by itself, so 넌 stays 반말 even with -요 on the end. Politeness lives in the ending (-요, -습니다) and in which words you pick — never in how many syllables they have.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: These short forms are the spoken sound written down — but watch the actual route. In speech 것 becomes 거, and only then do the particles fuse onto it: 거 + 이 → 게, 거 + 를 → 걸, 거 + 는 → 건. (Don't be fooled by the full forms: 것을 is pronounced [거슬], not [거를].) 뭘 takes the same route: 무엇 shrinks to 뭐 [무어 → 뭐], and then 뭐 + 를 → 뭘. And -지요 squeezes into one syllable as -죠, which is pronounced [조] — there is no 'y' glide in it, and after a 받침 it tightens: 춥죠 = [춥쪼].

drill.instruction: Say each sentence the way you would actually say it out loud — contract what can be contracted. Follow the model.
drill.model: 저는 학생이에요. → 전 학생이에요. · 이것이 좋아요. → 이게 좋아요. · 그렇지요? → 그렇죠?

englishSpeakerPitfall.wrong: Avoiding 전 / 거 같아요 / 이거 because they look like slang or 반말
englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 전 학생이에요. · 좋은 거 같아요. · 이거 주세요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English contractions ("I'm", "gonna") really do drop the register, so learners assume Korean works the same way and stick to 저는 / 것 같아요 / 이것 to stay polite. It backfires: in conversation the full forms sound like a textbook being read aloud. Politeness in Korean lives in the ending (-요, -습니다), not in the length of the word. What shortness does signal is informality — so let 전 and 거 같아요 do the talking, and keep 저는 and 것 같습니다 for interviews, emails, and essays.

exampleSentence.note: 점심 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating is directed at lunch
물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; the drinking action hits 물
한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; can also split: 한국어 공부를 해요
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book
일기 ends in vowel 기 → 를; writing is directed at the diary
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music
영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie
운동하다 has no object here — not everything needs 을/를; negative form: 운동 안 해요
Noun+하다 split negative: 일 + 안 + 해요 — the stop sign goes between noun and verb

exampleSentence.en: Are you eating? / Do you eat rice?
exampleSentence.note: 밥 ends in consonant ㅂ → 을; 밥을 먹다 is the most common eating phrase in Korean
커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를; 마시다 is directed at the drink.

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 물 ends in consonant ㄹ → 을; 많이 = a lot, modifying the verb
책 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; reading is directed at the book.
음악 ends in consonant ㄱ → 을; listening is directed at the music.
영화 ends in vowel 아 → 를; watching is directed at the movie.
매일 is a time adverb — it doesn't need a particle; it modifies the entire sentence

exampleSentence.en: I drink a lot of water.
exampleSentence.note: 많이 (adverb) modifies the verb directly — no particle needed on the adverb itself

extendedDialogue.setting: Jihee (지희) and her coworker Minho (민호) are chatting over lunch about their daily habits

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.en: Minho, do you eat breakfast every day?
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 먹어요 — 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ → 을; eating (먹다) is directed at breakfast

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: No, I don't eat breakfast. I'm busy.
lines.grammarNote: 아침을 안 먹어요 — the stop-sign 안 goes directly before 먹어요 (a pure verb, not noun+하다)

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 그래요? 저는 매일 밥을 먹어요. 물을 많이 마셔요.
lines.romanization: Geuraeyo? Jeoneun maeil babeul meogeoyo. Mureul mani masyeoyo.
lines.en: Really? I eat rice every day. I drink a lot of water.
lines.grammarNote: 밥을 먹어요 and 물을 마셔요 both use 을 because 밥 and 물 end in consonants. 많이 modifies 마셔요; it does not take a particle.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.en: I drink coffee. That's my breakfast.
lines.grammarNote: 커피를 마셔요 — 커피 ends in vowel 이 → 를 attaches; drinking is directed at coffee

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 — 한국어 ends in vowel 어 → 를; this is also valid as 한국어 공부를 해요 (split form)

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 네, 매일 한국어를 공부해요. 그런데 책을 안 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Ne, maeil hangugeoreul gongbuhaeyo. Geureonde chaegeul an ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Yes, I study Korean every day. But I don't read books.
lines.grammarNote: 한국어를 공부해요 uses 를 because 한국어 ends in a vowel. 책을 안 읽어요 keeps 을 on the object and puts 안 before the pure verb 읽어요.

lines.speaker: 지희
lines.ko: 저는 책을 읽어요. 그리고 음악을 들어요.
lines.romanization: Jeoneun chaegeul ilgeoyo. Geurigo eumageul deureoyo.
lines.en: I read books. And I listen to music.
lines.grammarNote: 책을 읽어요 and 음악을 들어요 both use 을 because 책 and 음악 end in consonants. Two clean object sentences.

lines.speaker: 민호
lines.ko: 좋아요. 오늘은 영화를 안 봐요. 책을 읽어요.
lines.romanization: Joayo. Oneureun yeonghwareul an bwayo. Chaegeul ilgeoyo.
lines.en: Good. Today I won't watch a movie. I'll read a book.
lines.grammarNote: 영화를 안 봐요 puts 안 before the pure verb 봐요. 책을 읽어요 keeps 을 because 책 ends in consonant ㄱ.

readingText.title: 수빈의 하루 일과 (Subin's Daily Routine)
readingText.body: 저는 매일 아침 밥을 먹어요. 커피를 마셔요. 회사에서 이메일을 써요. 보고서를 읽어요. 점심에는 동료들과 밥을 먹어요. 퇴근 후에는 음악을 들어요. 한국어를 공부해요. 드라마를 봐요. 주말에는 운동 안 해요. 그냥 책을 읽어요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: Every morning I eat a meal. I drink coffee. At work I write emails. I read reports. At lunch I eat with my coworkers. After work I listen to music. I study Korean. I watch dramas. On weekends I don't exercise. I just read books.

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do in the morning?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 먹어요 (eats a meal) and 커피를 마셔요 (drinks coffee).

comprehensionQuestions.question: What two things does Subin do after work?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 음악을 들어요 (listens to music) and 한국어를 공부해요 (studies Korean)

comprehensionQuestions.question: Find all the 을/를 in the text. For each one, explain why 을 or 를 is used — not the other form.
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밥을 (ㅂ consonant ending → 을), 커피를 (이 vowel ending → 를), 이메일을 (ㄹ consonant ending → 을), 보고서를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 밥을 (again, ㅂ → 을), 음악을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을), 한국어를 (어 vowel ending → 를), 드라마를 (아 vowel ending → 를), 책을 (ㄱ consonant ending → 을). The rule: consonant-ending nouns take 을, vowel-ending nouns take 를.

culturalNote.title: 밥 먹었어요? — The Korean greeting that's really about food
culturalNote.body: In Korea, one of the most common informal greetings is '밥 먹었어요?' (Have you eaten?) — said instead of 'How are you?' to close friends and family. Offering food is central to Korean social bonding. Answering 'yes' (네, 먹었어요) or 'not yet' (아직요) is totally normal. Notice that in this casual greeting, the particle 을 is often dropped: '밥 먹었어요?' rather than '밥을 먹었어요?' This is the natural particle-dropping that Koreans do in fast speech — but you now know the full form with 을, which makes the shortened form easy to understand.

inlineExercises.explanation: 아침 ends in consonant ㅁ, so it takes 을. 를 is only used after vowel-ending nouns. 이 and 가 are subject markers, not object markers — they mark who is doing the action, not what receives it.

커피 ends in vowel 이, so it takes 를. 을 is for consonant-ending nouns. 은/는 are topic markers, not object markers — they set the topic of the sentence, which is different from marking what is being drunk.

inlineExercises.prompt: 다음 문장을 자연스럽게 고쳐보세요: '저는 안 공부해요.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부하다 is a noun+하다 verb. In the everyday short negative, split it into 공부 + 안 + 해요. Pure verbs take 안 right before the verb (안 먹어요), but noun+하다 verbs usually split: 공부 안 해요, 운동 안 해요, 일 안 해요.
한국어 ends in vowel 어, so it takes 를. This is one of the most common sentences a Korean learner will ever say — 한국어를 공부해요 — so it's worth drilling until it's automatic.

inlineExercises.hint: 영화 ends in a vowel — which form of the object marker do you need? And 보다 is a pure verb, so where does 안 go?
inlineExercises.explanation: 안 goes right before the action verb to make a short negative. 영화 is the thing watched, so 영화를 stays as the object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly says 'I don't study' using the 안 negative?
inlineExercises.explanation: 공부 안 해요 is correct — noun + stop-sign + 해요. '안 공부해요' is wrong because 안 can't go before a noun-verb compound. '공부를 않아요' is missing the -지 needed for the long negative form (공부를 하지 않아요). '안 공부를 해요' mixes up the word order in an unnatural way.

inlineExercises.prompt: Your friend says '책을 읽어요.' What is the role of 을 in this sentence?
options: It marks 책 as the subject doing the reading.
It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
It marks 책 as a topic being discussed.
It is a verb ending attached to 책.
inlineExercises.correct: It marks 책 as the object receiving the action of reading.
inlineExercises.explanation: 을/를 is the object marker — it marks WHAT gets acted upon. 책 is what is being read. Subject markers (이/가) mark who does the action; topic markers (은/는) set what we're talking about. 을/를 is specifically for the thing that receives the verb's action.
읽다 is an action, and 책 is what you read, so it takes the object marker 을. 이 would mark 책 as a subject, not the thing being read.
하다 verbs become 해요 in polite present. 매일 makes this a normal present habit: 매일 한국어를 공부해요.
The time phrase comes before the object and verb. 커피 is what you drink, so 커피를 stays right before 마셔요.

bullets: 을/를 = ARROW from verb to object: consonant-ending noun + 을 / vowel-ending noun + 를
안 = STOP SIGN before a pure verb (안 먹어요); for noun+하다 verbs split it: noun + 안 + 해요
Key daily verbs with their objects: 밥을 먹다, 커피를 마시다, 한국어를 공부하다, 책을 읽다, 음악을 듣다, 영화를 보다

writingTask.prompt: Write 3 sentences about your daily routine: two things you do and one thing you don't do.
writingTask.hint: Mark the thing with N을/를 and use the present tense (먹어요, 마셔요); make one negative with 안 + verb.
writingTask.model: 저는 밥을 먹어요. 커피를 마셔요. 그런데 술은 안 마셔요.
writingTask.modelEn: I eat rice. I drink coffee. But I don't drink alcohol.

canDo: Mark what the action happens to with N을/를 (밥을, 커피를)
Say everyday actions in the polite present tense (먹어요, 마셔요)
Make a verb negative with 안 + verb (안 먹어요)
Choose 을 or 를 from the noun's 받침
